A system of linear equations is **consistent** if it has *at least one* solution. Otherwise, it is **inconsistent**.

Consistent systems, in turn, can be of the following two types:

- When a system of equations has a *single* solution, it is **consistent independent**.
- When a system of equations has an *infinite number* of solutions, it is **consistent dependent**.

We can summarize these definitions using the diagram shown below.

![](images/16/1692fbea298339ff839cf2f14986d51af45d1ec72b2b7d0de179336bdef40c0e.png)

The solutions of a linear system with two variables correspond to the points of intersection of the two lines defined by the equations. Three possibilities exist, as shown below.

![](images/8c/8c544df38ce82dd70c3d01718233c9fae1fae0534748892643a12b6556918fb7.png)

Remember that a system is *consistent* if it has a solution. So, the idea that a system of equations with no solution is *inconsistent* probably makes sense to you.

But what about the difference between consistent *dependent* and consistent *independent?* What is the reasoning behind these naming conventions?

To help understand consistent dependent vs. consistent independent, we'll look at some concrete examples:

- First, consider the following system.
$\left\{\begin{aligned}3x - y &=-2 \\ 6x - 2y &=-4\end{aligned}\right.$
This system has *infinitely many* solutions corresponding to the fact that the two lines coincide.![](images/e9/e9e98008aa5972889efdd3af0689da310c69bca06dd410a391a37e22aa8b0098.png)
In a previous lesson, we saw that the set of all solutions $({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{y}})$ can be expressed as
$({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{3x+2}})$
where ${\color{blue}{x}}$ is any number. Consequently, any ${\color{red}{y}}$-value in our solution is *dependent* on a corresponding ${\color{blue}{x}}$-value. Thus, the system of equations is consistent-*dependent*.
- Next, we consider the following system:
$\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=2x + 1 \\ y &=1 - x\end{aligned}\right.$
This system has a single solution corresponding to the unique intersection point of the two lines.![](images/bd/bd7edb530e16b853318a3e38785c7b6353c1b54f10ee3c4e2de7da915450f6d9.png)
The unique solution $({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{y}})$ is given by the single point $({\color{blue}{0}},{\color{red}{1}})$. In this case, the components of the solution do not depend on $x$ or $y$. Thus, the system of equations is consistent-*independent*.

The solutions of a linear system with two variables correspond to the points of intersection of the two lines defined by the equations. Three possibilities exist, as shown below.

![](images/8c/8c544df38ce82dd70c3d01718233c9fae1fae0534748892643a12b6556918fb7.png)

In other words, we have the following cases:

- If a system is *inconsistent* (has no solutions), the corresponding lines are parallel (do not intersect). And vice versa, parallel lines correspond to an inconsistent system.
- If a system is *consistent independent* (i.e., has exactly one solution), the corresponding lines intersect at exactly one point. And vice versa, intersecting lines correspond to a consistent independent system.
- If a system is *consistent dependent* (i.e., has infinitely many solutions), the corresponding lines intersect at infinitely many points (coincide). And vice versa, coinciding lines correspond to a consistent dependent system.

- If a system is *consistent dependent* (i.e., has infinitely many solutions), the corresponding lines intersect at infinitely many points (coincide). And vice versa, coinciding lines correspond to a consistent dependent system.

Consider a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix $M\mathbin{:}$


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=6 \\ y-3z &=-13 \\ -x-y-z &=-4\end{aligned}\right. \qquad M = \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -4\end{array} \right]
$$



We can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using the standard Gaussian elimination algorithm. The algorithm that we use is very similar to the case of $2 \times 2$ systems. 

Our goal is to create a descending "staircase" of $1$'s with $0$'s below, and we achieve this using elementary row operations. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & -6 & -24\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{6}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix is now in row echelon form, and we can apply back substitution to solve the original system of equations.

**Note:** The row echelon form of a matrix is *not* unique.  In the previous example, after the second row operation we arrived at



$$
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}{\color{red}1} & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & -3 & -13 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}-6} & -24\end{array}\right].
$$



This augmented matrix is already in row echelon form! However, it is always useful to do an extra step and obtain $1$'s along the main diagonal, like we did previously:



$$
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}{\color{red}1} & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & -3 & -13 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & 4\end{array}\right]
$$



Having $1$'s along the main diagonal makes the final back substitution process a little easier.

The **standard Gaussian elimination** for a $3 \times 3$ system can be described as follows:

- If $a_{11} \neq 0$ and $a_{11} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_1:=R_1/a_{11}.$

- We use first row and the necessary row operations to make the remaining entries of the first column below $a_{11}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{21} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2 + (-a_{21})R_1;$

- if $a_{31} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{31})R_1.$

- If $a_{22} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2/a_{22}.$

- We use the second row and the necessary row operation to make the entry below $a_{22}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{32} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{32})R_2.$

- If $a_{33} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3/a_{33}.$

- In some exceptional cases, such as when the element on the diagonal is equal to $0,$ we first need to exchange rows. Then proceed using the same steps as above.

Carrying out the above algorithm will convert the matrix to row echelon form.

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 3 & -6 & -3 \\ 0 & -4 & 12 & 36 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & 12 & 36 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & 12 & 36 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+2z &=1 \\ y-3z &=-9 \\ z &=1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$
y-3(1)=-9\,⟹\,y=-6.

$$
x-(-6)+2(1)=1\,⟹\,x=-7.
$$

Remember that we can represent a system of two linear equations in two variables using matrices. We can do the same thing for a system of three linear equations in three variables, such as the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x+2y\text{ }-\text{ }2z &=7 \\ 2x\text{ }-\text{ }1y\text{ }-\text{ }4z &=2 \\ 2x+1y\text{ }-\text{ }3z &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

For a $3 \times 3$ system like the one above, we put the coefficients of the system into a $3 \times 3$ coefficient matrix:



$$
A= \begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}3} & {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}-2} \\ {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}-1} & {\color{blue}-4} \\ {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}-3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$



Each row has the coefficients of one of the equations in the system, and each column consists of the coefficients of one particular variable.
We also have the $3 \times 1$ column vectors



$$
\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix}{\color{red}7} \\ {\color{red}2} \\ {\color{red}3}\end{bmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix},
$$



where $\mathbf{b}$ consists of each constant on the right side of the system and $\mathbf{x}$ contains the variables.
With these matrices, we can write our system as $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b},$ or



$$
\begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}3} & {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}-2} \\ {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}-1} & {\color{blue}-4} \\ {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}-3}\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}{\color{red}7} \\ {\color{red}2} \\ {\color{red}3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Some linear equations have **infinitely many solutions.** 

For example, consider the following equation: 

$$
x+5 = x + 5
$$

Let's attempt to solve this equation by subtracting $x$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & =x+5 \\ x+5-x & =x+5-x \\ 5 & =5\end{aligned}
$$

So, what does $x$ equal? The statement $5=5$ is *always* true, irrespective of the value of $x.$ This tells us that *any* value of $x$ is a solution to the equation!

Don't believe it? If we substitute any value, say $x=3,$ into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & =x+5 \\ 3+5 & =3+5 \\ 8 & =8.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

It's important to note that substituting *any* value for $x$ into the equation will lead to a true statement. For example, the values 

$$
x=42,\qquad x=-\dfrac 1 4, \qquad x=1.2345
$$

are *all* solutions to the original equation.

To summarize:

- Our original equation has *infinitely many solutions.*

- The solution of the equation is "*any (real) value of* $x$".

value:
Let's attempt to solve each equation in turn:

- For the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+1 & =4x+1 \\ 4x+1-4x & =4x+1-4x \\ 1 & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is true for all values of $x.$ Therefore, the equation $4x + 1 = 4x + 1$ has infinitely many solutions.

- For the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x & =-4x+6 \\ -3x+4x & =-4x+6+4x \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $-3x = -4x + 6$ has the unique solution $x = 6.$

- For the third equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+7 & =2x-1 \\ 2x+7-2x & =2x-1-2x \\ 7 & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is false for all values of $x.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

ax = bx,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. If $a = b,$ then the equation has infinitely many solutions.

$$
\begin{aligned}2x &=2x,\,\frac{1}{3}x=\frac{1}{3}x\,-2.16x=-2.16x\end{aligned}
$$

To show that the general equation $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b,$ we can substitute $a$ for $b$ in our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax & =bx \\ ax & =(a)x \\ ax & =ax\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we simplify this equation by subtracting $ax$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax & =ax \\ ax-ax & =ax-ax \\ 0 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The equation, $0=0,$ is always true, regardless of the value of $x.$ Therefore, the equation $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b,$ and any value of $x$ is a solution to the equation.

Consider the equation

$$
2qx = 10x,
$$

where $q$ is a constant. If we're given that this equation has infinitely many solutions, how can we find the value of $q?$

Notice that this equation is in the form $ax = bx{:}$ 

$$
\underbrace{2q}_{\large a} \ x = \underbrace{10}_{\large b} \ x
$$

In this case, 

$$
a = 2q, \qquad b = 10.
$$

We know that an equation of the form $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b.$ Therefore, the equation has infinitely many solutions if

$$
2q = 10.
$$

Solving this for $q,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2q & =10 \\ \frac{2q}{2} & =\frac{10}{2} \\ q & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $2qx = 10x$ has infinitely many solutions if $q = 5.$

We can check that this answer is correct by substituting $q = 5$ into our original equation. Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2qx & =10x \\ 2(5)x & =10x \\ 10x & =10x\end{aligned}
$$

and simplifying this equation by subtracting $10x$ from both sides yields

$$
\begin{aligned}10x & =10x \\ 10x-10x & =10x-10x \\ 0 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

which is true for all values of $x.$

**Note:** The constant $q$ in this problem is sometimes called a **parameter.**

Each of the following equations has infinitely many solutions:

$$
2x + 1 = 2x + 1, \qquad \dfrac13x -2 = \dfrac13x -2, \qquad 1-x = 1 - x
$$

More generally, suppose we have an equation of the form

$$
ax + b = cx + d,
$$

where $a, b, c,$ and $d$ are constants. Then, this equation has infinitely many solutions if 

$$
a = c\quad \text{and}\quad b = d.
$$

Note that if we substitute $c=a$ and $d=b$ into this equation, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}ax+b & =cx+d \\ ax+b & =(a)x+(b) \\ ax+b & =ax+b\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying this equation by subtracting $ax$ from both sides of the equation gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax+b & =ax+b \\ ax+b-ax & =ax+b-ax \\ b & =b\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation, $b = b,$ is always true. Therefore, the equation has infinitely many solutions, and any real value of $x$ is a solution.

$$

$$

We know that we can write a system of three linear equations in three variables in the form $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ where

- $A$ is the $3\times 3$ coefficient matrix,

- $\mathbf{x}$ is the column vector of variables, and

- $\mathbf{b}$ is the column vector of constants.

If the $3\times 3$ matrix $A$ is invertible, then we can find a solution to the system $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ by "pre-multiplying" both sides of the equation by $A^{-1}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =b \\ {A}^{-1}Ax & ={A}^{-1}b \\ {I}_{3}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\ x & ={A}^{-1}b\end{aligned}
$$

So, to find the solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ we simply calculate $\mathbf{x}= A^{-1}\mathbf{b}.$

Let's see how this works for a particular system in the next example.

The point $P$ consists of the coordinates $(x,y)$ that satisfy both equations $y=x+2$ and $y=2x+1.$ So, to find the coordinates of $P$ we need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=x+2 \\ y &=2x+1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We can solve this system by substitution. Substituting the first equation $y=x+2$ into the second equation $y=2x+1$ gives an equation that we can solve for $x\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =2x+1 \\ x+1 & =2x \\ 1 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

This is the $x$-coordinate of the point of intersection. To find the $y$-coordinate, we substitute $x = 1$ back into one of the equations, say $y=x+2,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x+2 \\  & =1+2 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=1, \, y=3.$ So, the point of intersection has the coordinates $(1,3).$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2y & =1 \\ 3+2y & =1 \\ 2y & =-2 \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}

Let's consider a system of linear equations where the corresponding coefficient matrix is singular. For example, consider the following system and its associated augmented matrix:


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=2 \\ 2x-y-z &=-1 \\ 2y-6z &=-10\end{aligned}\right. \qquad M = \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & -6 & -10\end{array} \right]
$$



To solve the system, we can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as usual. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & -6 & -10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -5 \\ 0 & 2 & -6 & -10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=2 \\ 0x+y-3z &=-5 \\ 0x+0y+0z &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final equation $0x+0y+0z = 0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of just two equations:



$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=2 \\ y-3z &=-5\end{aligned}\right.
$$



The **basic variables** are the variables of our system whose coefficients are the pivots of the row echelon form matrix. Let's illustrate the pivots of $M\mathbin{:}$



$$
M= \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & -3 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]
$$



The pivots are

- $m_{11}=1,$ which is the coefficient of $x,$ and

- $m_{22}=1,$ which is the coefficient of $y.$

Therefore, the basic variables are $x$ and $y.$

The remaining variables are called the **free variables**. We have only one free variable in our system, which is $z$.

Finally, we can describe the **general solution** by finding equations for the basic variables in terms of the free variables. In our case, this means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z$.

To do this, we apply the back substitution. From the second equation, we obtain

$$
y - 3z = -5
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	y = -5+3z.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-(-5+3z)+z=2\,⟹\, & x=-3+2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-3+2z \\ y &=-5+3z \\ z &=z\end{aligned}\right.
$$


where $z$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as


$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}= \begin{bmatrix}-3+2z \\ -5+3z \\ z\end{bmatrix}= \begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -5 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+z \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}, \qquad z\in(-\infty,\infty).
$$



Geometrically, this is the vector equation of a line, and any point on the line is a solution to our original system.

If we want to find some **particular solution** of the system, we simply choose some particular value of $z$ and find the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the line. For example, if we choose $z=0,$ then the corresponding values are $x=-3$ and $y=-5$ and the particular solution is $x=-3,$ $y=-5,$ $z=0.$

Suppose we want to solve the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y+z &=1 \\ y-z &=2 \\ z &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The augmented matrix for this system can be written as 

$$
M =
	\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}{\color{red}1} & 2 & 1 & 1 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & -1 & 2 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & 3\end{array}
	\right].
$$

Notice that the matrix is in *row echelon form* (or REF). Whenever the augmented matrix is in row echelon form, we can solve the system using a method called **back substitution**.

Back substitution involves

- starting with the lowest equation (which is already solved for one variable),

- substituting the result into the next-lowest equation to find the solution for another variable, and

- continuing to substitute the result into the next-lowest equation until the values of all the variables have been found.

Here, the third equation states that $z=3.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
y -(3) = 2 
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	y = 5.
$$

Now, we substitute both $y=5$ and $z=3$ into the first equation to get

$$
x + 2(5) + (3) = 1
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x = -12.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-12,$ $y=5,$ and $z=3.$ We can write it in vector form, as follows:

$$
\left\langle -12,5,3 \right\rangle = 
	\begin{bmatrix}-12 \\ 5 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

**Note:** The values $x=-12,$ $y=5,$ and $z=3$ together form *one* solution. We say that this system has *one* solution, *not* three solutions. A system with three solutions would have three different solution vectors, whereas here, we only have *one* solution vector.

A matrix is said to be **nilpotent** if some positive power of the matrix is the zero matrix. For example, the matrix

$$B = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$$

is nilpotent because its second power is the zero matrix:

$$\begin{aligned}{B}^{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\ & =O\end{aligned}$$

To state the definition more precisely: a matrix with the property $B^k=O$ for a number $k>0$ is known as a **nilpotent** matrix, and the lowest number $k$ such that $B^k=O$ is called the **index.**

Therefore, our matrix $B$ is a nilpotent matrix of index $2.$

Some linear equations can have **no solutions.** This means there is no value of $x$ that can be substituted into the equation to give a true statement.

For example, let's consider the following equation:

$$
x+1 = x
$$

Let's attempt to solve this equation. We start by subtracting $x$ from both sides.

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x \\ x+1\,-\,x & =x\,-\,x \\ (x-x)+1 & =(x-x) \\ 0+1 & =0 \\ 1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the final equation, $1=0,$ is always **false**. In other words, there is no value of $x$ that we can substitute to make the equation true. 

Therefore, our equation has no solutions.

In general, suppose we have an equation in the variable $x$ of the form 

$$
ax = b,
$$

where 

- $a$ and $b$ are constants, and

- $b$ is *not* equal to zero, which we write as $b \neq 0.$

Then, if $a = 0,$ the equation has **no solutions.**

Indeed, by substituting $a = 0$ into $ax=b,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}ax & =b \\ (0)x & =b \\ 0 & =b\end{aligned}
$$

which is a *contradiction* (i.e., a statement that's always false) because we were told that $b \neq 0.$ Therefore, the equation has no solution.

$$

a = 7q, \qquad b = -5.

$$
\begin{aligned}7q & =0 \\ \frac{7q}{7} & =\frac{0}{7} \\ q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the equation $7qx = -5$ has no solutions if $q = 0.$

**Note:** The constant $q$ in this problem is sometimes called a **parameter.**

where $a$ and $b$ are constants, and $b\neq 0.$ If $a = 0,$ then the equation has no solution.

First, we rewrite the equation in the form $ax = b.$ 

We start by adding $4x$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2nx+7 & =-4x+5 \\ 2nx+4x+7 & =-4x+5+4x \\ 2nx+4x+7 & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we subtract $7$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2nx+4x+7 & =5 \\ 2nx+4x+7-7 & =5-7 \\ 2nx+4x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we factor $x$ on the left-hand side. This gives

$$
(2n + 4)x  = -2.
$$

Notice that this equation is now in the form $ax = b{:}$

\underbrace{(2n + 4)}_{a}x  = \underbrace{-2}_{b}
$$

Therefore, the equation has no solution if

$$
2n + 4= 0.
$$

$$

$$
